title: Facing the Dutch: White's mainline squeeze against the Leningrad

objective.summary: Your opponent chose the Dutch: they spent king cover to buy the e4 square and a kingside attack. The mainline answer is the fianchetto squeeze — c4, g3, Bg2 — aiming your bishop at the light squares ...f5 abandoned, castling into a structure their storm cannot easily reach, and denying the one break (...e5) their whole system is built for.

planClasses.label: Clamp with d5 when ...e5 is finally ready
planClasses.description: The timing plan: let Black spend four moves preparing ...e5, then answer the last preparation with d5, fixing the centre where the g2 bishop and the c-file both smile. Position-specific to this tabiya — the clamp only works because ...c6 just spent a tempo.

planClasses.label: Expand with Rb1, b4-b5
planClasses.description: The patient plan: while Black's pieces all face e5, the queenside pawns walk. Rb1 first because the fianchettoed g2 bishop stops watching b1's diagonal duties, then b4-b5 opens files where Black has no pieces.

planClasses.label: Trade off the g7 bishop
planClasses.description: The Leningrad's king cover IS the fianchetto: remove the g7 bishop and the dark squares around the king belong to nobody. The reusable doctrine lives in the shape entry; this pack only declares the target.

annotations: The most popular answer at your band, and the principled one: stake the centre Black declined to contest. One third of your peers already play it — the rest of this pack makes the follow-up as automatic as the first move.
The system move: your bishop is heading for the h1-a8 diagonal, where ...f5 stopped guarding e4 and d5 forever. Every Dutch player fears this bishop more than any attack.
Onto the square that vetoes ...e5. Black's entire setup will now work to overload this knight's watch.

Castle behind a wall their storm cannot easily reach: with g3 played, ...f4 has no lever and the g2 bishop guards the king while attacking the queenside. Compare this with castling into a KID storm — same pawns, opposite story.
Development with a threat behind it: the knight watches d5 and e4, and quietly prepares the e4 break — the move that turns Black's missing f-pawn into a permanently airy king.
The Warsaw finisher: ...e5 is fully queued. This is YOUR decision point — clamp it with d5, or ignore it and expand with Rb1/b4. Both are authored; the comparison is the drill.

The clamp: ...e5 now costs an en-passant-shaped concession or never comes, the g2 bishop's diagonal stays open through c6's newly created hole on d6, and Black's four preparation moves ask what they were for.
The expansion: concede ...e5 will come, meet it with dxe5 when it does, and start b4-b5 where no Black piece is looking. The walked continuation ...Na6 9.b4 shows the pawns rolling.
The London-style answer — second most popular at your band (18.1%). A different pack's system; it is here so choosing it is a decision, not a default.
The Staunton Gambit: a pawn for open lines against the weakened king, played in 4.0% of games at your band. Sharp, respectable, and a memory battle — the opposite temperament to this pack's squeeze.

checkpoints.label: 6.O-O — your king is safe from the storm they wanted
7...c6 — clamp with d5 or expand with Rb1: choose
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 3.Nc3 (9.2% at the family root) develops toward the e4 break before the fianchetto. A real alternative order whose main cost is allowing ...d5 setups where the c3 knight bites on granite.

5.Nh3 aims the knight at f4/g5 instead of vetoing ...e5 from f3 — the idea catalogued in the Leningrad Carlsbad row (under the 2.g3 order). It trades the veto for attacking squares; whether the veto was worth more is exactly what playing both here should show you.

8.e4 is the third plan played immediately, and the 2026-08-15 engine pass priced it: at depth 22 it is 1.65 worse than 8.Qb3 and 0.73 worse than the spine's 8.d5, and the recapture this note previously asserted — 8...fxe4 9.Nxe4 — drops a piece, because after 9...Nxe4 the knight on e4 is defended by nothing (the g2 bishop's diagonal is blocked by its own knight on f3). The unsupported walked line has been removed rather than replaced; no alternative ninth move is authored here.

feedbackClaims.text: At the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), the Dutch position after 1.d4 f5 was reached 4,845,395 times and White scores 49.8% against 46.0% — and this pack's 2.c4 is already the most common answer (33.3%), ahead of 2.Bf4 (18.1%) and 2.Nf3 (15.1%).

The Leningrad has one break and its name is ...e5: a White move is working here almost exactly when it adds a watcher of e5, restrains the break's preparation, or opens play somewhere the break cannot help.
...f5 never goes home: whatever else happens, the e6 square, the g4 square and the h5-push hook are features White can aim at for the whole game — the Dutch player accepted them on move one.

graduationBlockers: There is no pack review workflow in this system and there never will be one (owner ruling 2026-08-13). Only a citable source or mechanical validation that bears on the claim clears a blocker.

First-move alternatives (2.Bf4, 2.e4) cannot be deviations in a follow_theory pack — no spine node precedes ply 1 — so they are sibling root branches. Third attestation of wave-2 friction #3; the format should bless the idiom or grow a start-anchor.

The trade-the-g7-bishop plan is a hands-off declaration: the authored spine never begins Be3/Qd2/Bh6, so the shapePlan reference names a target the drill does not reach (wave-2 friction #5 pattern, noted honestly).

ENGINE-CHECKED 2026-08-15 for the comparison, not for the claim. The two authored plans are within a tenth of a pawn of each other and of the engine's preference: 8.d5 is 0.08 below 8.Qb3 and 8.Rb1 is 0.15 below, so the pack's 'both are authored, the comparison is the drill' framing survives. The 'hole on d6' assertion is a structural claim no evaluation addresses and it stays ungrounded. The pass also refuted this pack's third plan: deviation #2's authored walked line 8.e4 fxe4 9.Nxe4 drops a piece (-3.11), and the line was removed rather than replaced.
Whether d5 or Rb1 is more common or scores better at these bands is unquantified below the family root.
